Very soluble in water; practically insoluble in dehydrated al- cohol and in ether. Profile Inositol, an isomer of glucose, has traditionally been considered to be a vitamin B substance although it has an uncertain status as a vitamin and a deficiency syndrome has not been identified in man. Sources of inositol include whole-grain cereals, fruits, and plants, in which it occurs as the hexaphosphate, fytic acid. It also occurs in both vegetables and meats in other forms. The usual daily intake of inositol from the diet is about 1 g. It is an ingredi- ent of numerous vitamin preparations and dietary supplements, and of preparations promoted for a wide variety of disorders. Inositol appears to be involved physiologically in lipid metabo- lism and has been tried, with little evidence of efficacy, in disor- ders associated with fat transport and metabolism. It has been investigated in the treatment of depression and anxiety, in diabet- ic neuropathy, and in neonatal respiratory distress syndrome and retinopathy of prematurity. Neonatal respiratory distress syndrome. Inositol supple- mentation has been tried in premature infants with respiratory distress syndrome (p.1508). A meta-analysis1 found that infants given inositol had improved survival and lower rates of bron- chopulmonary dysplasia and retinopathy of prematurity than those given placebo. 1. Howlett A, Ohlsson A. Inositol for respiratory distress syndrome in preterm infants. Available in The Cochrane Database of Sys- tematic Reviews; Issue 4.
